p: On the Friday after the written, Abby put a chair in the middle of the briefing room, sat Jordan in it, stood behind the whiteboard with her arms folded, and said she was an F-16 and she was annoyed. Jordan had to explain what Biscuit would do if the F-16 rocked its wings and turned slowly left. She did. Abby rocked the whiteboard eraser back at her, which was apparently the fighter saying thanks.

The chart legend took two evenings at the club table with a highlighter and the reading glasses she claimed she only needed for medication labels. NTSB 830 took one, out loud, as a lawyer, with Abby playing the hysterical passenger holding up a finger that was absolutely, definitely, broken. A simple fracture of a finger is not a serious injury. Jordan said it eleven times. On the twelfth she said it like she believed it, and Abby opened the logbook to the endorsement page.

Jordan's logbook, endorsements. 01/21/27. I certify that Jordan E. Reyes has demonstrated satisfactory knowledge of the subject areas in which they were deficient on the Private Pilot Airplane airman knowledge test.. /s/ 01/21/27 A. Strand 3418862CFI RE 06-30-2027
That's A.2. A.1 and A.37 come at the end, after the prep. The prep has to be inside the two calendar months before the month you test, so we don't start it until we know the month. Which means Walt.

Walt had known every examiner on the Front Range for thirty years, and he had opinions about all of them, most of which he'd keep to himself until you bought him a breakfast burrito. Jordan bought him two at the counter by the FBO on a Tuesday in January. He ate one, wrapped the other in a napkin for later, and wrote a name on the napkin.

Kendra Lowe. Flew freight for twenty two years, night, in airplanes older than Biscuit. She asks you what you'd do, and then she asks why, and then she waits. You'll want to fill the quiet. Don't. She's fair. She isn't fast. He folded the napkin over the name. I'll call her.

He did. It took him a couple of weeks, because Kendra booked out like a dentist, and Walt didn't text Jordan until he had a date he liked. It came in on a Sunday morning, February 7, while she was standing in the bay at the end of a twenty four with a mop in her hand.
A text from Walt Herrera. Kendra Lowe. Friday March 19. 0730 at the FBO briefing room. After that she's full into May. Don't make me call her back.

No question mark. Jordan read it twice, the way she read everything from Walt, and then she did the math she'd been not doing since September. The year ran out in the second week of April. March 19 left a little under four weeks of margin for weather, a broken airplane, or a bad day. It was enough. It was not a lot.
She propped the mop against the wall and looked at the calendar on her phone, at March, and at the twenty first, that she'd been not looking at since the first of the year.

Monday, February 8, ten in the morning, the tie down. She'd slept, she'd eaten, and she'd driven to the airport instead of calling anybody, which was what she did now when she wanted to think. Biscuit sat in the cold with her cover on and her tail rope frosted white.
Jordan opened the left door, sat sideways in the seat with her boots on the ramp, and looked up at the panel.

The card above the mag switch had been there since November, white IV tape at the corners, the HI DAD sticker peeking out from under the bottom edge. Her capitals, seven lines. Halfway down, the one she'd written on purpose so she would never have to decide it again: EMOTION IS WEATHER. MARCH AND NOV 5: DUAL OR NOTHING. And at the bottom, the one that held the rest in place: I DON'T CHANGE THIS CARD IN THE PARKING LOT.

A checkride wasn't dual. Kendra wasn't her instructor. Kendra would be sitting in the right seat with a clipboard, and Jordan would be the pilot in command of an airplane on the twelve month anniversary of the worst phone call of her life, give or take two days. Walt had picked a good slot. Walt didn't know what was in March. Or maybe he did, and he'd decided she'd tell him if it mattered.
Her phone was in her hand. Walt's text was still on the screen. Don't make me call her back.

She texts Walt: Give me until tonight. He answers in a minute. Fine. At two o'clock she and Abby sit at the club table with a fresh index card between them. Abby asks one question, what a March rule would be for, and then doesn't talk for a long time. Jordan answers it: it's for the days she can't trust herself to tell. Not for the month. For the days. They work it out in pencil on the fresh card, and at 4:10 she texts Walt one word. Yes.

That evening at her kitchen table she copied it onto a new card in pen, the way they'd worked it out in pencil, and then she drove back out and taped it up herself, on top of the old corners, with fresh IV tape.

The new index card, taped above the mag switch. J. REYES. PERSONAL MINIMUMS. MINE, NOT THE FAA'S, NOT ABBY'S.. SOLO, KAPA PATTERN: CEILING 3,500 AGL. VIS 6 SM. WIND 10, GUSTS 5 OVER, CROSSWIND 5. IF IT'S CLOSE, IT'S NO.. 7 HOURS OF SLEEP OR I DON'T GO. NO SOLO THE MORNING AFTER A SHIFT.. NOTHING TO DRINK FOR 12 HOURS. SICK OR TAKING ANYTHING, I DON'T GO.. EMOTION IS WEATHER. MARCH AND NOV 5: DUAL, OR AN EXAMINER IN THE RIGHT SEAT.. THE WEEKEND OF MARCH 21: NOTHING. NOT EVEN THE AIRPORT.. IF I CAN'T SAY OUT LOUD THAT I'M FIT, I CALL THE NIGHT BEFORE.. ONE FACTOR: ADD 500 FT, 1/2 MILE, TAKE 5 KNOTS OFF. TWO FACTORS: GO HOME.. I DON'T CHANGE THIS CARD IN THE PARKING LOT.
Abby had made her read it out loud twice at the table, and then said the old line had been a good rule for October, and this was a better one for March.
Then the back page of the logbook, because two numbers were still open.

Jordan's logbook, back page: 61.109(a), as of 2/8/27. TOTAL 61.1 (40) DUAL 53.2 (20) SOLO 7.9 (10). 2.1 TO GO.. XC DUAL 4.4 NIGHT 5.6 NIGHT FULL STOPS 12 HOOD 3.1 SOLO XC 5.1 LONG SOLO XC TOWERED CHECKRIDE PREP 3.0 WITHIN 2 CAL MONTHS: 0.0. JAN, FEB, OR MAR COUNT FOR A MARCH TEST.. SOLO ENDORSEMENT (A.7) 1/6/27, 90 DAYS.. KNOWLEDGE TEST 1/12/27: 95 A.2 1/21 A.1, A.37: AT THE END.

Abby had blocked out the prep: February 17, March 4, March 10, March 16, all dual, all on days that came after a full night of sleep, which she'd worked out from a photo of the station fridge. The solo time was Jordan's to plan.

Down in the flight bag, folded soft along the creases, was Danny's 2018 sectional, the one with the coffee ring on Castle Rock and the pencil lines going out from Centennial like spokes. Moab. Steamboat. And one short straight line northeast, to a magenta circle with tick marks around it, at a town called Akron. Eighty four miles, give or take. A little less than an hour each way. She'd measured it once already, in January, and hadn't told anybody.

Thursday, February 11: 1.2, slow flight over the reservoir until the stall horn chirped and quit and chirped and quit on command, then six short field landings on 35R with Abby's point, the first stripe past the numbers, written on her kneeboard. Tuesday, February 23: 1.1, the same, plus steep turns until the bump of her own wake came through the floor twice. She writes both in the logbook in ink and doesn't update the back page until she's added it twice.

Monday, March 15, 6:50 in the evening. Daylight saving time had started the day before, which meant Jordan had lost an hour of sleep the night before a 24 and never gotten it back, and the sun was still up over the mountains when she came out of the grocery store. Her phone rang in the parking lot. Abby never called. Abby texted, in three parts.

I got it. She didn't wait for Jordan to ask what. The regional. The number with the weird area code in January was the recruiter. I interviewed in February and didn't tell you, because you had a written and then you had a checkride and I'm a professional. Offer came this afternoon. Class starts Monday the 22nd, out of state. I fly out Sunday.

She'd crossed fifteen hundred hours on a Tuesday in March and told nobody. Jordan stood in the parking lot with a bag of groceries on her hip. A cart rolled past her on its own, slowly, toward a Honda.

Your checkride's Friday. I'll be at the fence. I'm flying your last prep tomorrow. After the flight I sign A.1 and A.37, and your recommendation in IACRA. So that's fine. A pause. I'm telling you before I tell my mom. That's not a pep talk. It's a fact.

Abby. That's huge. Congratulations. Then: You said in April I'd get a handoff, your notes, and a CFI you trust. If it snows Friday, who's that? A short laugh on the line. You remember that. Of course you do. Tuesday after the prep flight, Abby hands her a printed page with a name and number on it, Gabe at the north end, and her training notes in a clear sleeve, and signs both endorsements in green while Jordan watches the pen.

Friday, March 19, 7:24 AM. The FBO's second briefing room had a round table, four chairs that didn't match, a window onto the ramp, and a whiteboard somebody had cleaned badly, so that the ghost of a holding pattern was still on it. The sky outside was a low flat gray, and the windsock was out straight from the northeast.

Weather, printed at 7:05 AM. METAR KAPA 191253Z 03009KT 10SM OVC025 M01/M04 A3021 RMK AO2. TAF KAPA 191120Z 1912/2012 03010KT P6SM OVC025. FM191600 03014G22KT 2SM -SN BR OVC012. FM192000 02015G25KT 3/4SM SN OVC006. FM200500 36010KT 3SM -SN OVC015
Upslope. She'd seen it Tuesday in the forecast discussion and Thursday on every channel. Daylight time now, UTC minus six, so the snow was due at ten.

Kendra Lowe came in at 7:29 with a rolling bag, a laptop, a thermos with a fishing lure sticker on it, and a gray braid down her back. She was somewhere in her fifties, compact, with reading glasses pushed up into her hair, and she shook hands like someone who'd decided long ago not to make a production of it. Jordan. Kendra. Sit wherever you like. We'll start with paper, because paper is where people lose the most time.

She paid Kendra's fee first, by check, the number Walt had told her in February with the face he used for weather. Then the paper. Kendra pulled up the application in IACRA with the FTN and turned the laptop so Jordan could see it. Photo ID. The student pilot certificate, plastic, a little bent. The medical. The knowledge test report, out of its sleeve, and Kendra ran her thumb over the raised seal the way the proctor had. The logbook, open to the endorsements, A.2 from January and A.1 and A.37 from Tuesday in Abby's green.

Jordan's logbook, endorsements. 03/16/27. I certify that Jordan E. Reyes has received and logged training time within 2 calendar months preceding the month of application in preparation for the practical test and they are prepared for the required practical test for the issuance of a private pilot certificate.. /s/ 03/16/27 A. Strand 3418862CFI RE 06-30-2027. 03/16/27. I certify that Jordan E. Reyes has received the required training in accordance with 14 CFR 61.107 and 61.109. I have determined they are prepared for the Private Pilot Airplane Single-Engine Land practical test.. /s/ 03/16/27 A. Strand 3418862CFI RE 06-30-2027

Then 61.109, line by line. Kendra read each number off the application and found it in the logbook herself. Total. Dual. Night. Hood. The long solo cross-country. Prep: four flights with Abby, February 17 and three in March, 4.6 hours. Then solo.
Application says solo 10.2. Your back page says 10.1. She said it the way you'd mention someone's shoelace was untied.

Let me add it. She runs a finger down the solo column out loud, the way she reads back a drug and a dose. The October solo. November. December. Limon. February 11, 1.2. February 23, entry 1.1, summary 1.0. The summary's wrong. 10.2. The application's right. She corrects the back page in ink, one line through the old number, initials it. Kendra watches, then writes something down. The back page is yours. The entries are the record. Good.

8:20 AM. Kendra had read the airplane's records for half an hour, the annual, the ELT, the transponder, and the AD list with the selector line now in Marisol's ink, done January 5, next due at 100 hours on the tach. She asked about the left fuel cap from December. She asked what Biscuit's door did. Then she closed the binder.
Walt tells me you've been planning a trip for a while. Where is it?
Akron. Colorado Plains Regional. My niece, and her mom in back.

Then that's our scenario. Say you passed today. It's a couple of weeks from now, a Saturday morning. You, your niece in the right seat, her mother in the back. Full tanks. Show me the airplane can do it. She pushed a blank weight and balance form across the table. Start with people.
Jordan had done this worksheet more times than she could count since August, on the hood of Claire's car, on the club table, once on a napkin. This time a stranger was watching the pencil.

I weighed them Saturday. Marisol's scale. Ellie was 79 with her shoes on, the seat cushion's 3, Claire's 174. I'm 162. Forty gallons. She does it in pencil and Kendra checks every line with a calculator. 2,156 pounds, CG 43.18, forward limit 37.06 at that weight, 144 under gross. Why weigh a seat cushion? Because it's in the airplane. Kendra comes very close to smiling. Not quite. Next: where does the CG go as the fuel burns off? Forward, a little; fuel sits aft of it. Then Akron's runway, and the PAPIs.
By nine the oral had a rhythm. Kendra asked. Kendra waited. The heater ticked.

She did the intercepts first, as promised. What do you do if a fighter shows up off your left wing, a little ahead, and rocks its wings? Jordan said: rock hers back to acknowledge, and follow it. Squawk 7700 unless ATC says otherwise, and try to call on guard, the emergency frequency, with who she is and where. A climbing turn of ninety degrees or more away from her, without crossing her path, means she can go. Circling the airport and overflying the runway means land there. Kendra made her do the hand motions. Jordan felt ridiculous and got every one.

Then the chart. Kendra put her finger on the magenta circle northeast of Denver, the one with tick marks around it and a small star. Jordan said: magenta means no tower. The ticks mean fuel and the field's attended during normal working hours. The star means a rotating beacon, sunset to sunrise. She checked it against the chart supplement entry for Akron on her tablet while Kendra watched, and said attended eight to five, beacon, 100LL around the clock by card. Kendra nodded once.
Then she turned the sectional over, so it was just paper.

Akron. You've landed and shut down. Ellie's getting out on her side. She's on the step, she slips on frost, and she lands on her hand. Her wrist is broken. Claire's an ER nurse, so you know it's broken. What is that, and what do you do?
It was the question. Jordan knew it the way you know a rhythm on a monitor. A passenger with a broken bone, the one she'd answered as a paramedic in January.

She says it slowly. It's an accident under 830.2. It happened between boarding and when everyone has gotten off, and she hadn't gotten off. A broken wrist is a serious injury, because the only fractures that aren't are simple ones of fingers, toes, and the nose. So after Ellie's taken care of, I notify the NTSB immediately, under 830.5, and file the report within 10 days under 830.15. And I don't move the airplane. Kendra writes for a while. Your report said you missed this one. I answered it as a medic. And now? Now I answered it as the pilot.

10:25 AM. The oral had run two hours and fifty five minutes, and Kendra had just said the words Jordan had been waiting for since February: That's the ground portion. You passed it. She'd said it the way she said everything, without decoration, and then she'd looked out the window.

Jordan looked too. The ramp had gone soft and gray. The mountains had been gone since nine. Snow was coming sideways past the light poles, small and dry and determined, and the windsock was standing out stiff from the northeast.

Weather, printed at 10:12 AM. METAR KAPA 191553Z 03014G21KT 2SM -SN BR OVC011 M02/M04 A3018 RMK AO2. METAR KCFO 191553Z 03016G24KT 1 1/2SM -SN BR OVC009 M03/M04 A3017. TAF KAPA 191520Z AMD 1915/2012 03014G22KT 2SM -SN BR OVC011. FM191900 02016G26KT 1/2SM SN FG VV004. FM200500 36010KT 3SM -SN OVC015
Eleven hundred feet. Two miles. Gusts to 21 and building. The amendment had brought the worst of it in an hour early, which was what amendments did on days like this.

She'd looked at a sky like this one in December, at the tie down, with her mother's birthday on the other end of it. She'd turned around then with the tanks full. It had been the cheapest place to do it, and she'd never once wished she'd gone.
Kendra turned from the window. You're pilot in command of that airplane today. Are we flying?

We're not flying. Eleven hundred feet and two miles, gusts building, and the amendment brings it down by one o'clock. I don't want to fly maneuvers under that, and I don't want to be the pilot who tried. Can I get a letter of discontinuance for the oral? Kendra's already opening her laptop. You can. Under 61.43(e), for weather. Area I's done. You'll keep it for 60 days. She looks at Jordan over the screen. For the record, I was going to say no too. I like it better when I don't have to.

Letter of Discontinuance, 03/19/2027. APPLICANT: JORDAN E. REYES. PRACTICAL TEST: PRIVATE PILOT, AIRPLANE SINGLE-ENGINE LAND. DISCONTINUED 03/19/2027, WEATHER (14 CFR 61.43(e)(2)). AREAS OF OPERATION SATISFACTORILY COMPLETED: I. PREFLIGHT PREPARATION. CREDIT FOR COMPLETED AREAS IF THE REMAINDER IS PASSED BY 05/18/2027 (61.43(f)). PRESENT THIS LETTER WHEN THE TEST RESUMES.. /s/ K. LOWE, DPE

Kendra had a cancellation, Monday, March 22, at eight, and she offered it. Jordan had looked at Monday for a long time Friday afternoon, at the weekend sitting in front of it, and then at her card. The weekend was nothing, not even the airport, and Monday wasn't the weekend. She'd said yes.
Friday night, at 9:52, a text from Abby.

A text from Abby Strand. Called the airline. There's a class on the 29th. I'm in it. That's a week I'm buying for me, not for you, so don't thank me. I'll be on the ramp Monday at 8. Don't make it weird.

Sunday was a year. She came off a twenty four at seven. They went to the nine o'clock Mass at her mother's church in Aurora, all of them, and then to Claire's, where Ellie had a game at two in the slush and played the whole thing at the back like a wall, and nobody watched the sideline, and everybody watched the sideline. Jordan didn't go to the airport. She'd written that down.

Monday, March 22, 7:05 AM. Clear, still, minus four, the sky scrubbed blue the way it only got after an upslope storm, and eight inches of new snow on everything that wasn't the ramp. Marisol had swept Biscuit's wings Sunday afternoon and put the cover back on. Overnight the cold had found the gap at the tail.
Weather, printed at 6:58 AM. METAR KAPA 221253Z 34006KT 10SM CLR M04/M09 A3034 RMK AO2. TAF KAPA 221120Z 2212/2312 VRB04KT P6SM SKC. FM221800 34010KT P6SM FEW120

Kendra walked out with her at 7:20 and stood at the tail with her thermos while Jordan worked down the checklist, reading each line and touching each thing. She didn't say anything. Every so often she looked at something Jordan had just looked at.

Over by the FBO door, behind the painted line, three people were standing in the cold with coffee. Walt was at the fence by the gate, collar up, in the spot he'd stood in since September. Abby was by the door with her hands jammed in her jacket. And next to her, in the good maroon cardigan under a long wool coat, with a scarf wound twice around her neck, stood Jordan's mother, who had never once come to watch Danny take off. Not in eleven years. Walt had gone and picked her up in Aurora at six thirty. Jordan had found that out from Claire, by text, at 6:41.

At the tail she ran a glove along the top of the horizontal stabilizer. White. Sometime overnight the cover had flapped loose at the back. So: frost, stabilizer and elevator both, thin, gritty, like a nail file. Right wing too, a gray strip along the trailing edge. You could miss it from six feet. Up close it looked like 220 grit.

Frost on the stabilizer and the right wing. I need twenty minutes. Maybe thirty. Kendra nods, takes her thermos, and finds some sun to stand in. Before Jordan can even finish asking, there's Marisol, brush in one hand, towels in the other. (Hangar door. She'd been watching since 7:15.) Brush, towel, then Jordan's bare hand over every square foot of both wings and the tail, Abby's rule from October, until her fingers hurt and then a bit past that. Clean. The checkride starts thirty one minutes late. Over by the FBO her mother checks her watch, opens her mouth, shuts it.

8:31 AM. Engine start. Mixture, throttle, prime, master, the beacon, clear prop, and Biscuit coughed twice in the cold and caught. Taxi to Alpha. Runup near the departure end of 35R, mags, carb heat, the door latches, the top one on her side twice. Kendra watched her do the top one twice and didn't comment. Jordan told ground she was ready for departure, and ground told her to monitor tower.

She briefed the exchange of controls out loud before they took the runway, the way the ACS wanted it, three steps, you have the flight controls, I have the flight controls, you have the flight controls. Kendra said it back to her. Then tower cleared Niner One Echo for takeoff on 35R.

Full power. Ten thousand feet of runway in front of her, and in air this cold and dense Biscuit needed about a tenth of it. She rotated at fifty five. The door stayed shut. Over the left wing as she climbed, the FBO slid by and she could see three small figures on the ramp, and one of them had a hand up, and it wasn't Walt's, because Walt's was at the fence, and it wasn't Abby's, because Abby never waved at anything.

Right turn east. Climbing to seven thousand five hundred. She said it out loud, the way she'd been saying it since July. Shelf at eighty. I'm staying at seventy five. Flight following with Denver Approach, radar contact, which wasn't a yes to anything. The Aurora Reservoir under the left wing, a sheet of white ice with a black crack across it. BEND, her turn point from November, on the GPS and out the window at the same time. Then northeast, on Danny's line.

First checkpoint: on time, almost to the minute, which felt like cheating. At the second one she checked groundspeed. Eleven point two miles, six minutes fifteen. She did it in her head. Kendra did it on a calculator. A hundred and seven. Same number, so nobody had to say anything.
East of Strasburg. I-70 under the left wing, a truck stop, snow on the fields in long stripes where the plow had thrown it. Kendra closed the binder.
New information. Akron's six hundred overcast now. Going down, not up. Where to?

Diverting to the Space Port. Left turn, already rolling into it while she's talking. The Space Port is out there to the west, a gray cross on white, big enough to see from here. Level. Then the arithmetic. About fourteen miles, two eighty true, call it two seventy five magnetic. Into this wind maybe a hundred knots. Eight or nine minutes, about a gallon. Under the seven thousand floor before I get close, so I'm starting down to sixty five hundred now. Then Denver, then the ATIS. Kendra writes for the length of the descent.

The Space Port tower gave her a right base for 35. Eight thousand feet of runway with snow banked along both edges like the sides of a bobsled run. Kendra asked for a soft field landing, so Jordan flew it like the runway was mud: a little power in the flare, nosewheel held off as long as the elevator would hold it, then the soft field takeoff, nose high, off in ground effect, level, accelerate, climb. Kendra didn't say anything. Kendra wrote.

Hood on. East, out past the ten mile ring, under the eight thousand floor, into a sun she couldn't see. Straight and level. A climb. A descent. Turns to headings. Then Kendra said, Close your eyes and put your head down, and flew the airplane somewhere unpleasant, and said, Your airplane. Jordan opened her eyes on a nose low left bank with the airspeed climbing. Power back. Level the wings on the attitude indicator. Ease the nose up to the horizon. In that order, which Abby had made her say out loud forty times in January until it bored her, which was the point.

Hood off. An emergency descent. Then, over a white quarter section with a farm road along one side, Kendra pulled the throttle to idle and said the engine had quit, and Jordan had the nose at sixty five knots before Kendra's hand was back in her lap, picked the field upwind of the road, flew the checklist, and had them set up for a landing in the snow by the time Kendra said, Good. Go around.

Slow flight at seventy five hundred, with the stall horn chirping, held within forty feet. A power off stall. A power on stall, the left wing trying to drop and her right foot telling it not to. Steep turns: left, lost forty feet; right, gained sixty, felt her own wake bump through the floor, rolled out four degrees past east and fixed it. Turns around a center pivot buried in snow, the wind drifting her toward the road until she steepened the bank downwind. Kendra didn't say anything about any of it. By then Jordan had decided that was a compliment.

Back to Centennial. A forward slip to a landing on 35R, left wing down and right rudder in, the nose pointed off the runway and the airplane dropping like an elevator, straightened at the flare, down on the second set of stripes. A go-around Kendra called at two hundred feet, power, carb heat in, flaps up in steps, climb. Then tower cleared them for the option, and Kendra said the last thing on her list.
Short field. Your point is the numbers. On them, or no more than two hundred feet past.

Final. Sixty knots, flaps forty, the 35 parked dead still in the windshield. Still is good. Still means you hit it. Then at two hundred feet a bump off the snowbanks picked Biscuit up from underneath. Sixty nine knots. Twenty feet high. And the numbers started sliding, down the glass, under the cowling, gone. Float. She knew it before the airspeed did, the way you know a pressure's dropping a beat before the cuff cycles.

Going around. Full power, carb heat in, nose to the climb attitude, flaps up to twenty, then ten, then up, positive rate. She tells tower. Kendra writes something while they climb. The second approach she flies ready for the bump and holds the numbers still on the windshield, and the mains go down ten feet past the 35 with the stall horn singing, and she stands on the brakes like the POH says to. Why'd you go around? I was going to land long. And I wanted to. Kendra nods. The second one is why we do this.

The last landing was a normal one, full stop, inside the 400 feet with room to spare. On the rollout Kendra looked out her side window for a while, at the snow along the edges going gold in the sun, and then she said, Taxi us in.

Jordan's hands had a little shake in them. She read the after landing checklist out loud anyway, flaps up, carb heat cold, transponder, lights, and turned off at Alpha and told ground where she was going.

Ahead of her, past the FBO, her mother was standing behind the painted line with Abby and Walt. She'd been standing there for two hours and six minutes. Abby would say later that she hadn't sat down once. Jordan brought Biscuit around toward the tie down at a walk, feet on the brakes. Halfway through the turn her mother stepped over the painted line. One step. Two. Hands out a little, palms up, the way she used to come at you when you were six and had fallen off something. Looking at Jordan's face through the windshield. Only at that.
Not at the propeller. Gray blur, idle, about eight feet in front of her.

Brakes. Mixture, cutoff. Checklist later. Her left hand goes flat on the windshield, palm out, the scene hand, the one that keeps a bystander from walking into a car wreck. Eyes on her mother's eyes. Lourdes stops. Engine quits. Blade swings past twice, ticks, and sits. Only then does Jordan run the rest of the shutdown out loud, mags, master, the ELT check she did a beat late and says so. Kendra glances out at Lourdes. Back at Jordan. That's postflight, she says.

Thirty seconds, maybe. Her mother came across the concrete to the strut. Nothing about the propeller, not one word, and from her mother that was a small miracle. Church coat. An FBO visitor sticker slapped on it crooked, Walt's work probably. I never came for him. I thought if I watched him go up, I'd have to watch him come down. Jordan still had the tie down rope. She kept holding it. So I watched you come down. Then her mother reached up and fixed her collar, which was fine, it was always fine, and walked back behind the paint to Walt.
At the round table Kendra printed it out of IACRA, signed it, and slid it across without ceremony, which Jordan would remember as the most ceremonious thing anybody had ever done for her.

Temporary Airman Certificate. UNITED STATES OF AMERICA. DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORTATION. FEDERAL AVIATION ADMINISTRATION. TEMPORARY AIRMAN CERTIFICATE. THIS CERTIFIES THAT JORDAN E REYES. HAS BEEN FOUND TO BE PROPERLY QUALIFIED TO EXERCISE THE PRIVILEGES OF. PRIVATE PILOT. RATINGS AND LIMITATIONS: AIRPLANE SINGLE ENGINE LAND. ENGLISH PROFICIENT. DATE OF ISSUANCE: 03/22/2027. THIS TEMPORARY CERTIFICATE EXPIRES: 07/20/2027 (120 DAYS, 14 CFR 61.17). EXAMINER: K. LOWE, DPE

Then Kendra did something she hadn't done in one long morning: she leaned back and put her reading glasses on top of her head. Your report said you missed the NTSB question in January. Friday you got it, and you knew why. I've had applicants answer every question as somebody else. A pilot they admire. An instructor. A brother. She capped her pen. You answered mine as you. Go take your niece to Akron. Weigh her first.

Walt was waiting in the hangar, on Marisol's rolling stool, in his canvas jacket. He'd held up nine fingers at the fence as she rolled by on Alpha, and put them away. Now he stood up in stages and handed her an envelope with nothing on the front. Inside was one page from the Hangar Six club agreement, the page with the clause on it, one year from the date of transfer, and in the margin, in two pens and a photo: CONDITION MET. 03/22/2027. W.H. M.T. R.K. Russ had initialed it from Phoenix, by photo, and Marisol had printed the photo and stapled it on, because Marisol.

It's your share, Walt said. It's been your share since a night in December when you drove to Pueblo. I'm slow, and I like paperwork. He looked at the envelope and not at her. In April I offered you book value. I'd like to take that back now, officially. If you ever sell it, sell it to somebody who reads the remarks.

Abby left on Sunday, March 28. On Saturday afternoon she came by the hangar with her flight bag already packed for good and stood next to Biscuit for a minute with one hand flat on the cowling, like you'd check a horse. Then she gave Jordan a pen. The green one. The one with the chewed cap that had signed every line in Jordan's logbook since April.

Endorsements are green. That was my thing. Remarks are yours, so I don't care what color you use, but you don't have a pen you like, and that's unacceptable. She zipped her jacket. Send me a picture from Akron. Not of the pie. Of her, in the right seat. At the door she turned around. You were the student I was going to log and forget. I read the lesson. Then you know the rest. Don't make it weird. She went. Jordan stood in the hangar holding a pen, which, she understood, was a pep talk.
Saturday, April 3, 9:40 AM, the tie down. Clear and still and cool, the mountains back where they belonged, the snow gone from the ramp and lying in gray rags along the fences.
Weather, printed at 9:05 AM. METAR KAPA 031453Z 34006KT 10SM CLR 05/M06 A3016 RMK AO2. METAR KAKO 031455Z AUTO 31008KT 10SM CLR 04/M07 A3011 RMK AO2

She did the passenger line in her logbook the way she'd once done a run report, every box. Three takeoffs and three landings in the preceding 90 days, same category and class, as the sole manipulator: four on March 22. Day, so 61.57(b) didn't come into it. Temporary certificate, photo ID, medical, in the flight bag's inside pocket with a zipper. Weight and balance on the clipboard: Ellie weighed that morning on Marisol's scale, 79 again, in the sneakers, the seat cushion on top, Claire at 174, full tanks. 2,156. CG 43.18. Plan in pencil, KAPA to BEND to Akron, seventy five hundred under the shelf and nine thousand five hundred after it, because the course was 053 magnetic and nine five was odd plus five hundred and more than three thousand feet above the plains.

The card above the mag switch had a new line at the bottom, written Wednesday night at her kitchen table, in Abby's green pen because it was the one she had: WITH PASSENGERS: ADD 500 FT AND 5 KNOTS. DAY ONLY TILL I'VE FLOWN 20 HRS AS PIC. BRIEF EVERYONE, EVERY TIME. Under the shelf she still stayed three hundred under or lower, Abby's rule, unless she heard the words cleared into the Bravo. Some limits she'd keep because they were good.

Claire was in the back seat, behind the right seat, with her coat in her lap and Danny's old Hangar Six cap on her own head for once. At Christmas she'd made the deal out loud: if you pass, she sits up front, and I sit where I can see her. Now she sat there, belted, and looked out the window at the hangars like they owed her money, and then, when she thought nobody was looking, like they didn't.

And in the right seat, on Marisol's cushion, which bought her about four inches, sat Ellie, in a purple fleece zipped all the way up, with her chin higher than the glare shield. She could see over the panel. Tall enough to see over the panel, in pencil, on the last page of his logbook. She could see the nose, and the runway past the nose, and the mountains past that, Pikes Peak way off to the south with snow on it. She'd gone completely quiet when she realized it, which for Ellie was a medical event. Jordan let her have it. Thirty seconds, maybe. Nobody said anything, not even Claire.

On her head was Danny's headset. The gray one, D.R. scratched into the headband with a key, the cracked ear seal with the black tape Marisol kept meaning to replace and never did. Jordan had cinched it down to the smallest notch it had and folded a bandanna under the band, twice, and Ellie held it on with both hands anyway, like it might get up and leave. The boom mic sat about an inch off her lip, which was close enough. It was still too big for her by about a size and a half, and she could not have cared less. Jordan wore the club loaner, the blue one with the sticky volume knob. It pinched behind her ear. Fine.

Jordan turned around in the left seat and did the briefing, all of it, the ACS list with 91.107 up front. Pilot in command: me. Belt: flap up to open, tab in till it clicks. Harness over the collarbone, not the neck, on the whole time the wheels are turning. The door does a thing at takeoff if the top latch isn't set, so I set it twice and you get to watch me do it. Quiet means quiet when I say so, important stuff included, except traffic, which you call like a clock, two o'clock high, that kind of thing. Nobody walks around the front of the airplane. Not with the prop turning, not with it stopped, not ever. Feet flat on the floor, off the pedals. The yoke in front of you moves when mine moves. Let it. It's not haunted.
Then the emergency part. Claire got there first. Jordan caught it on her face a half second before Ellie let go of the headset and swiveled on the cushion until she was looking dead at her aunt.
What if your heart stops? Like Daddy's.

Probably never. Real answer? After Daddy, all of us got our hearts checked. Mine's normal. Then the FAA doctor listened to it for, like, a weirdly long time, and signed a paper saying so. If I ever feel funny up there, I land, and I tell you why after. She unhooks the hand mic and walks her through it the way she's walked a hundred scared husbands through what happens next, on their own living room floors, short words, one thing at a time. If Jordan stops talking and Ellie can't wake her up, this button. Hold it down, say help, say the numbers on the side. Somebody's listening the whole time and they answer. Plus Mom's right there. Ellie takes the mic in both hands, thumb parked next to the button, not on it. Niner One Echo, she says, quiet, nothing keyed. That's us. Jordan hangs it back on the hook. Claire, in the back seat, is staring out at a hangar like there's going to be a quiz.

Runup on Alpha, near the end of 35R. Mags. Carb heat. Door latches, top one twice. Ellie saw the second one and kept quiet, as briefed, with a face that wasn't quiet at all. Jordan told ground she was ready for departure. Ground told her to monitor tower.

10:21, cleared for takeoff. Full power. Fifty five, nose up, door shut. And Ellie, breaking a rule she'd been given ninety seconds earlier, whispered, You said it does a thing. Not if you latch the top.

Right turn east. Seventy five hundred. She said the shelf thing out loud, for Ellie's benefit this time, and Ellie said it back. SHELF AT EIGHTY, in a robot voice, for some reason. Reservoir off the left wing, the ice on it gone gray and rotten at the edges. BEND. Then northeast, on his line, and twenty seven miles later the Class B was behind them and Jordan let Biscuit climb, slowly, in the cool morning air, to nine thousand five hundred.

From nine five the plains don't end. Brown, white, brown. Center pivots, dozens, all the same size. Snow hanging on in the north side of every draw. A coal train somewhere off the left wing, on the line toward Akron, that Jordan watched for five minutes and couldn't swear moved. Ellie had both hands clamped on the headset and her nose about an inch from the glare shield.
Cold air. Thick. Honestly? Best day she's had since October.
Ellie thought about that. She's not out of breath. From the back, a laugh. Claire's real one. Then a cough, to cover it, which fooled nobody.

Akron came up out of the brown at 11:02, a small grid of streets and a grain elevator and, a mile north, a long gray runway that looked like someone had ruled it on the prairie with a straightedge. No tower. She announced on the common frequency at ten miles and again on the downwind, left traffic for 29, and nobody answered, because nobody else was flying to Akron at eleven on a Saturday in April. Seven thousand and one feet, wind nearly down the centerline. She flew the pattern like there was an examiner in the right seat. There was, kind of. Mains on the numbers. Nose down, gentle. And from the back seat Claire, of all people, said, Huh.

The FBO had a courtesy car. Old Buick, coffee smell, and on the dash a hula girl wearing a tiny pilot's cap that someone had made out of tape and a bottle cap. The man behind the counter handed over the keys without asking for anything but a first name, and told her the diner was on Main, and to get the cherry if they had it, and not to tell them he'd said so, or they'd think he was sweet on somebody.

It was the kind of diner Jordan had seen a hundred of on calls in small towns east of the city: a counter with eight stools, booths along the windows, a pie case by the register with a handwritten card in front of every pie. Cherry, yes. Also a coconut cream, and Ellie stood in front of the case looking at it for long enough that the waitress came over to see if she was okay. Claire ordered for the table, three slices, two coffees, a chocolate milk with a bendy straw, and when the waitress asked if it was a special occasion Claire said yep, my sister-in-law's first flight as a pilot, and my kid's first time riding up front. Then she quit talking for a second and Jordan watched her decide, the way you'd watch somebody decide whether to pull a second dose. My husband planned it. He didn't get to come. The waitress didn't make a thing of it. When she came back with the forks there were four, and she laid the extra on the empty side of the booth, across from Ellie, and went off for the pot. Nobody touched that fork the whole hour, and nobody moved it either.

Was the test lady nice? Ellie got that out around a mouthful of coconut cream. Jordan said fair, and that fair beat nice. Ellie chewed on it, and the pie, and allowed that Coach was fair. So the test lady was basically Coach, then.

Jordan texted Abby the tie down picture, Ellie up on the cushion with the headset on and her chin clear of the panel by a good two inches. Four minutes, and back it came, from a hotel near the training center. Tall enough. Told you. Now eat the pie.
Her mother, next. Jordan called from the booth, half a slice still on her plate, Ellie picking the cherries off Claire's one at a time with her fingers.

I know. Claire sent me a picture of the baby in the front. Behind her Jordan could hear the whole kitchen. The radio on the counter, some call in show about lawns, and the lid on the pozole pot doing its little rattle, the one it had always done. Is it good, the pie?

A long breath on the line. Your brother talked about that pie for three years. He never took me. Then a different kind of quiet. The kind where she was standing at the stove deciding something, wooden spoon in her hand, and you'd better not interrupt. Ask me again in the summer. When it's warm. I'm not saying yes. Jordan opened her mouth. Too slow, as usual. Call me from Centennial. Not the car.

Back at the airport Claire took the envelope from Christmas into the FBO to pay for the fuel, the share they'd worked out on the back of it in December, and then went to find the restroom, and then, Jordan suspected, went to stand somewhere for a few minutes by herself. That left the two of them in Biscuit on the ramp, Jordan in the left seat with the door open and her boots on the step, Ellie in the right on her cushion, the headset around her neck now.

Jordan took the green notebook out of the flight bag. She'd known the last page was there since April. She'd turned to it once, the first week, and seen KAPA and KAKO in pencil, and closed the notebook on her finger, and put a paper clip on it, the way she had with the solo page. Saving it. She took the clip off now.

Danny's logbook, the last page, in pencil. Feb 28. NOT FLOWN YET.. KAPA to KAKO. 84 nm. 9,500 after the shelf.. Pie at the diner.. Take Ellie when she's tall enough to see over the panel.. Bring Jordan.. (Pencil so I can change the date.)
She read it to Ellie out loud. The parentheses too. Bring Jordan came out wrong, a little high, and she let it. Ellie didn't move.
Well, you came. Ellie checked the cabin, the ramp, the elevator over town, like taking attendance. And me. So that's done.
Jordan sat with that. Then, because Ellie had asked her a hard question that morning and she'd answered it straight, she decided to answer the one nobody had asked.
El. The first day I ever flew Biscuit, after, I came back out here by myself and sat in this seat for ten minutes. Didn't touch anything. Didn't tell anybody why.

I didn't know then. I thought I was deciding about the airplane. I wasn't. I'd just found this notebook in the door, with the Tums and his pencil, and it smelled like his car in here, and it was the last place I knew where he was still exactly how he was. She ran her thumb along the cracked green spine. I was saying goodbye to your dad. I just didn't know that's what it was. I'd never been at the end before, with him. I'm always at the end, at work. I wasn't there for his.
Ellie was quiet for a while. Out on the county road a pickup went by. Two fingers up off the wheel, at an airplane. People do that out there.
What are you doing now? In the ten minutes.

Jordan looked at the panel. At the card in its IV tape, her capitals, the new line at the bottom in green. At the HI DAD sticker underneath it, nine year old purple, one corner up the way it had been up since she'd first pressed it down in November, and every time since.

Ellie reached over and pressed the corner of the sticker flat with her thumb. It stayed down. It was the first time it had stayed down. Neither of them said anything about it, and they sat there for the rest of the ten minutes, not flying anywhere, watching the light go flat and bright across the prairie toward the mountains, which from here were only a faint blue line along the bottom of the western sky.

When Claire came back Jordan had her own logbook open on her knee, the one she'd bought for twelve dollars in April, the only thing in aviation that is. Every dual line in it had Abby's green ink at the end of it. This line was hers. She uncapped Abby's pen.

Jordan's logbook, 04/03/27. DATE 04/03/27. C172N N4791E. FROM KAPA TO KAKO. TOTAL 0.9. ASEL 0.9. PIC 0.9. DAY LDG 1.. REMARKS: First passengers. Ellie, right seat, on the cushion. Claire, back. Ellie could see over the panel. Pie at the diner on Main, cherry and coconut cream. The plan was in pencil, in the door pocket.. Brought Jordan.
She looked at it for a while. It was a good entry. It was hers. She'd read every line of it twice before she wrote the last one, which was a habit she was going to keep.

Danny's notebook went into the right door pocket, with a pencil. Not the left one, where she'd found it. The left door pops if you forget the top latch, and she wasn't trusting a year of his pencil to a latch. It had ridden in her flight bag for a year, and that was long enough. His could live in his airplane. Hers went home with her.

Top latch. Twice. Claire in back, Ellie up on the cushion with the gray headset and both hands on it again. Then the briefing, all of it, again, because every flight with people in it gets one. At the emergency part Ellie beat her to it. Hold the button. Say help. Say Niner One Echo.
Clear prop. Akron traffic, Cessna Niner One Echo, departing runway 29, Akron. Nobody answered. You say it anyway. Then she took her family home.
